newsitem.title: UK: British mad cow disposal may take 13 years - Labour.
newsitem.headline: British mad cow disposal may take 13 years - Labour.

text.p: The opposition Labour Party warned on Monday that Britain faced a huge problem in disposing of cattle slaughtered to tackle mad cow disease and it could take 13 years to incinerate all the carcasses.
"The remains of one million cattle slaughtered in last year's cull are waiting to be destroyed," deputy leader John Prescott told a news conference.

He said research by Helen Jackson, a Labour member of parliament's Environment Committee, had shown that by January less than four percent of the cattle slaughtered last year had been disposed of by incineration.

Meanwhile, the government was using 41 cold stores, 11 warehouses and locations such as the container port in his own Hull, eastern England, constituency to store carcases and rendered-down meat and bonemeal.
Britain has been forced to slaughter all cattle aged 30 months or older following evidence that people could catch a human form of mad cow disease by eating infected meat.
It has now agreed an additional cull of some 100,000 animals which may be vulnerable to the disease in an attempt to get a European Union ban on British beef exports lifted.

Prescott said Britain had just three incinerators capable of disposing of cattle carcasses at sufficiently high temperatures to destroy the prion proteins associated with mad cow disease, or Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).
Only one of these, near Southampton in southern England, has so far been given a contract to dispose of carcasses, he said.
"At this rate. it will take to the year 2010 to dispose of last year's cull," Labour said in a statement.
Jackson told the news conference that Conservatives on the Environment Committee had blocked her proposal for an inquiry into the problems of carcass disposal and storage.
She said a Labour government, which could be elected in Britain at an election widely expected on May 1, would set up such an inquiry, taking evidence in public.
